options: Observers learned the container-opening technique only after many attempts of their own.
Learning was more likely when the observer and the demonstrated animal appeared to belong to the same species.
Octopuses of a different species cannot solve container problems even when trained directly.
The control group performed worse than the trained octopuses did in the original demonstration.
explanation: 答案B。文中指出观看同种章鱼演示的章鱼几天内学会了打开容器，而对照组观看的是“不同物种、装在陌生容器里的章鱼”，没有显示出类似改进，并强调“the effect appears to depend on the perceived similarity between the observer and the demonstrated model”，可推断相似性越高越可能学会。A与“without any trial-and-error feedback”矛盾，C、D文中均未涉及。

passage: The Andes mountain range spans nearly nine thousand kilometers along the western edge of South America, and its structure records more than one hundred and fifty million years of plate interaction. At its core lie the high peaks of the Western Cordillera, in many cases volcanoes fueled by the subduction of the Nazca plate beneath the South American plate. East of the high peaks, geologists have identified a different architecture: a high plateau, the Altiplano, composed of layered volcanic deposits and ancient sandstones that record a time when the region was still at or below sea level. Notably, the Altiplano was uplifted later than the central peaks; isotopic dating of its rocks indicates that much of its present elevation was achieved only in the last six million years. This two-stage construction is one reason the range contains such a wide variety of rock types, and it helps explain why ancient lakebeds now sit at altitudes exceeding four thousand meters, preserving salt crusts that mining companies now harvest.
question: According to the passage, what distinguishes the Altiplano from the peaks of the Western Cordillera?
options: The Altiplano reached most of its present altitude far more recently than the central peaks.
The Altiplano lies west of the Western Cordillera and was formed at sea level.
The Altiplano contains no ancient sandstones, unlike the Western Cordillera.
The Altiplano consists mainly of volcanic rocks formed by subduction activity.
explanation: 答案A。文中明确写道“the Altiplano was uplifted later than the central peaks; isotopic dating of its rocks indicates that much of its present elevation was achieved only in the last six million years”，即阿尔蒂普拉诺高原大部分高度是最近才获得的，晚于中央山峰。A混淆了西科迪勒拉火山带，C方位错误（高原在东），D与“composed of layered volcanic deposits and ancient sandstones”直接矛盾。

passage: Pulsars were discovered in the late 1960s when radio telescopes detected brief, regularly spaced flashes of radio energy from objects far too dense to be ordinary stars. Their leading explanation soon became compelling: the flashes are lighthouse-like beams emitted by neutron stars, stellar remnants in which an entire sun's worth of matter has collapsed into a sphere only about twenty kilometers across. As such a star spins—some complete a full rotation in less than a tenth of a second—the beams sweep past Earth, and each time a beam points our way the radio telescope records a pulse. Remarkably, the interval between pulses is so steady that certain pulsars keep time more accurately than the best atomic clocks on Earth, which has led astronomers to use them as natural probes of gravity and as precise beacons for detecting the faint ripples of passing gravitational waves. The first confirmed detection, made in 1967 by a graduate student scanning chart recordings, was initially dismissed as a statistical fluke, but the repeating pattern soon proved impossible to explain by known astrophysical phenomena, and the discovery earned its discoverers a Nobel Prize within seven years. Today their precise timing is used to test general relativity, to monitor the rotation of the Earth's crust, and even to probe the interior structure of neutron stars.
question: What is the main idea of the passage?
options: Neutron stars are the densest objects in the universe and have yet to be fully observed.
Pulsars are spinning neutron stars whose steady beams make them useful as extremely precise clocks.
Radio telescopes were invented in order to detect the gravitational waves produced by collapsing stars.
The pulses from pulsars occur less frequently than the ticking of atomic clocks.
explanation: 答案B。全文围绕脉冲星是快速旋转的中子星（“the flashes are lighthouse-like beams emitted by neutron stars”）展开，并以“keep time more accurately than the best atomic clocks”“use them as natural probes”收束，B概括了主题。A过度推断，“最致密”未提；C因果颠倒，射电望远镜先于脉冲星发现；D与“full rotation in less than a tenth of a second”及原子钟对比不符。

passage: In the decades following Pavlov's classic experiments with dogs, researchers began to ask whether the same principles of conditioning operated in humans. Some early studies produced inconclusive results, because laboratory settings made it difficult to trigger strong emotional responses reliably and to measure them precisely. A breakthrough came when psychologists studied a small group of individuals who had received polio vaccinations as children. Decades later, when researchers presented the smell of the hospital where the injections had been given, several participants developed measurable sweat and heart-rate responses that had not been present before the treatment years earlier. Because the hospital smell had reliably co-occurred with the unpleasant sensation of the injection, it had acquired the ability to elicit a bodily response on its own. The finding demonstrated that classical conditioning can persist for decades and can operate through the sense of smell, which people often assume they cannot learn from.
question: According to the passage, what was unusual about the reaction of the vaccination participants?
options: They reacted to the smell of the hospital even though the injections had been given years earlier.
They had never received the vaccinations, yet showed symptoms of the disease.
Their responses appeared only after researchers tested them several times.
Their heart rates slowed down when the smell was presented.
explanation: 答案A。文中写道“Decades later, when researchers presented the smell of the hospital... several participants developed measurable sweat and heart-rate responses”，且注射是“years earlier”，说明他们对医院气味的反应在多年后依然出现。B错在“never received”；C“only after tested several times”文中未提；D方向相反，文中是反应增强而非减缓。

passage: The anthropologist Robin Dunbar proposed that the limits of human social groups are shaped by the capacity of the brain to track the relationships between individuals. In great apes, the size of a stable social group appears to scale with neocortex size, so researchers predict that larger neocortices should permit larger groups. When this pattern is applied to humans, Dunbar arrived at a figure of roughly one hundred and fifty people, a number he argued matches the size of cohesive groups observed in hunter-gatherer societies, and indeed the average number of acquaintances a typical person can list from memory. The figure—often called the “Dunbar number”—has also been detected, he claims, in more recent structures: the typical medieval village, the typical infantry company, and, perhaps not surprisingly, the upper limit at which employee email lists tend to become unwieldy. Critics, however, point out that the statistics behind the estimate are themselves inconsistent, and that the chains of evidence from primates to villages to email lists are uneven in quality.
question: The word “it” in the passage most nearly refers to
options: the average number of acquaintances a typical person can list
the pattern of relationship-tracking in great apes
the upper limit at which email lists become unwieldy
the figure of roughly one hundred and fifty people
explanation: 答案D。定位句为“a number he argued matches... and indeed the average number of acquaintances... The figure—often called the 'Dunbar number'—has also been detected, he claims...”。“it”对应的先行词是前文反复指代的“roughly one hundred and fifty people”这一数字，该数字被验证于村庄、连队、邮件列表。A是它的一个证据而非指代对象；B、C属于干扰项。

passage: Economists often distinguish between what a country produces in a given year, measured as gross domestic product, and what its citizens actually have to spend, measured as disposable income. The difference matters because a large portion of production is devoted to goods that will not be consumed in that year: factories building factories, warehouses filling up with inventory, and so on. Several developed economies have recently experienced episodes in which gross domestic product grew steadily while household spending stagnated. To explain this puzzle, analysts cite a set of factors that do not appear in the gross figure at all. First, companies have been paying back debt rather than expanding. Second, the share of income flowing to profit rather than wages has widened, and profit earners save a much larger fraction of what they receive. Third, household savings have climbed because retirement accounts are growing and because home prices have fallen in some regions. The point, the analysts stress, is not that the growth is an illusion but that the gross number conceals where the value goes.
question: Why does the author mention that companies have been paying back debt?
options: To suggest that gross domestic product measures debt repayment as a form of production
To explain why income available to households has not kept pace with overall economic output
To argue that debt repayment is more important than household spending for growth
To show that companies prefer paying down loans to expanding their inventories
explanation: 答案B。该句出现在解释“GDP增长但家庭消费停滞”之谜的三个原因中：“To explain this puzzle, analysts cite a set of factors... First, companies have been paying back debt rather than expanding.”偿还债务使价值留在企业部门，推不出流入家庭，故用于说明家庭可支配收入没有跟上总产出。A与“do not appear in the gross figure at all”矛盾；C、D文中无依据。

passage: Painting portraits of the dead was common in Renaissance Europe, but the conventions that governed such work changed sharply during the fifteenth century. Earlier portraits tended to place their subjects against plain backgrounds and to present them in rigid, frontal poses that emphasized the individual's status rather than his personality. From the 1460s onward, however, painters working in Florence and Venice introduced a new informality. They placed the sitter in a recognizable room or garden, sometimes turned the figure slightly away from the viewer, and recorded small personal details—the specific ring on a finger, the worn leather of a glove—details that suggested the painting had been made from direct, careful observation of that particular person. Witnesses noted that sitters sat for many hours, often on different days, so that the painter could choose the hour of light that flattered the subject's complexion. Some patrons, in turn, asked to be painted looking not at the viewer but at a distant point, a compositional choice that gave the finished work a quietly watchful character.
question: According to the passage, one effect of the new informal portrait conventions was that
options: plain backgrounds were reintroduced to improve the lighting
sitters preferred to be painted in frontal poses
portraits were less likely to emphasize the sitter's social standing
patrons no longer needed to sit for their portraits
explanation: 答案C。文中指出早期的 rigid、frontal 姿态“emphasized the individual's status”，而1460年代后的新风格“introduced a new informality”，通过真实环境、侧身姿态和个人细节“suggested... direct, careful observation of that particular person”，即重心从身份转向个人特质。B与“sat for many hours”矛盾；C错，新风格强调可识别的环境而非素净背景；D与“turned the figure slightly away”相反。

passage: Game theorists have long used a simple model, the prisoner's dilemma, to study why cooperation is difficult among self-interested individuals. In the basic two-person version, each player can cooperate or defect; both do best when both cooperate, but each player is tempted to defect, because defection pays more when the other player cooperates. Repeated play, economists have shown, can sustain cooperation if interactions are ongoing and players remember past behavior. Yet a series of computer tournaments pitted strategies against one another and found that the most successful approach was not endless revenge for past slights nor unconditional kindness, but a mix: begin cooperatively, cooperate again when the opponent cooperates, and respond to defection with a brief period of defection of one's own. Sociologists who study real organizations note that the same pattern shows up in labor negotiations and supplier relationships, where firms cooperate on most deals but maintain a visible capacity for retaliation that keeps partners honest.
question: It can be inferred from the passage that in computer tournaments, a strategy that punished every defection without limit most likely
options: defeated the mixed strategy in every round of play
performed no better than unconditional cooperation
produced cycles of retaliation that reduced its own payoff
was the only strategy able to sustain long-term cooperation
explanation: 答案C。文中说获胜策略不是“endless revenge for past slights”而是混合策略——对背叛只以“a brief period of defection”回应，暗示无限报复策略失败；结合博弈论背景，持续报复会引发对方持续报复，形成循环并降低自身收益，C为合理推断。A、B、D文中均无依据，且与“most successful approach... a mix”相矛盾。

passage: Bioluminescence—the production of light by living organisms—appears in surprisingly many unrelated groups: deep-sea fish, jellyfish, fireflies, and certain species of plankton. In the deep ocean, where sunlight cannot penetrate, the ability to make light solves several different problems at once. Some animals use light as a lure to draw prey into striking range; others use it to disguise themselves, matching the faint glow from above so that predators below cannot see their silhouettes. A third use is alarm: certain squid and shrimp, when grabbed by a predator, eject a glowing cloud of ink, blinding the attacker and creating a distraction that allows the animal to escape. The chemical reactions behind all of these displays vary, but they share one feature: the light is produced with almost no waste heat, making bioluminescence one of the most energy-efficient forms of light generation in nature. The phenomenon fascinated sailors for centuries before science explained it, and even today the mechanisms that control when an animal switches its lights on and off remain only partially understood. Researchers studying the bioluminescent systems of deep-sea creatures have discovered that some species can adjust the color of their light to match the ambient conditions of the surrounding water, while others flash in patterns too rapid for the human eye to follow. These adaptations suggest that bioluminescence evolved independently many times, and each lineage has fine-tuned its own chemical machinery to suit a particular ecological niche.
question: As used in the passage, the word “eject” most nearly means
explanation: 答案D。根据语境，乌贼和虾在被捕食者抓住时“eject a glowing cloud of ink”，其目的是“blinding the attacker and creating a distraction that allows the animal to escape”——把发光墨云喷射出去才能致盲攻击者并制造掩护，因此 eject 意为“喷出、排出”，对应 expel。absorb（吸收）、detect（探测）、reflect（反射）均不符合方向。

passage: Long-distance trade in the American Southwest dates back at least to the first millennium, and the ruins of a community called Chaco Canyon suggest that by the eleventh century the region had become a node in a network reaching into present-day Mexico. Excavations there have uncovered jet, a shiny black gemstone mined only on the Gulf Coast of Mexico, along with macaws and turquoise from the far north. What makes Chaco unusual, however, is not merely that foreign goods reached it, but that its elite households seem to have controlled the distribution of those goods to other communities. The largest of these houses, now called great houses, contain hundreds of rooms built around enormous central rooms and rooms with doorways so large that they could not have been used for individual access. Archaeologists believe such spaces served ceremonial purposes, and that access to the exotic goods stored there was governed by the ranking of the person involved, not by simple proximity to the canyon. In effect, distance from Chaco became a kind of currency: communities far from the center received the most prestigious items.
question: According to the passage, which of the following is true of the great houses at Chaco Canyon?
options: Some of their large central rooms were probably used for ceremonies.
Their doorways were unusually small so that access could be restricted.
They were built earlier than the eleventh century and therefore predate the trade network.
They were primarily residential buildings for ordinary families.
explanation: 答案A。文中写道大型住宅“contain hundreds of rooms built around enormous central rooms”并指出“Archaeologists believe such spaces served ceremonial purposes”。A错，精英控制分配、非普通家庭住宅；C与“doorways so large”方向相反；D时间错误，贸易网络在eleventh century 已存在。

passage: Astronomers who study the outermost reaches of the solar system have recently gained a new tool: a probe launched in the 1970s that is now more than fourteen billion kilometers from the Sun. Unlike earlier missions, which aimed at individual planets, this spacecraft was designed to sample the environment of interstellar space itself, and it has spent the past two decades crossing a boundary region called the heliopause, the surface where the Sun's own wind of particles finally gives way to the flow of material from beyond the solar system. One of the most striking discoveries came from measurements made just after the spacecraft entered this region: the radiation levels it recorded were far lower than theorists had predicted, a discrepancy that has forced researchers to revise their models of how the galactic medium interacts with the Sun's magnetic bubble. The spacecraft is gradually slowing down, and its data will become sparse as its power wanes, but its builders have fitted it with a recording system that can retain observations for years, in the hope that later missions may find it and recover the stored archive.
question: As used in the passage, the word “sparse” most nearly means
explanation: 答案B。前文“The spacecraft is gradually slowing down... its power wanes”说明探测器动力衰减，导致它发出的数据越来越少；因此 sparse 意为“稀少的、不多的”，与 scarce 同义。irregular（不规律）、faint（微弱，多指信号强度）、distorted（失真）均不如 scarce 准确。

passage: Mountain building on the deep ocean floor is far more active than most people assume, and the mid-Atlantic ridge provides the clearest picture of it. The ridge stretches nearly across the entire ocean, and along much of its length magma rises from below, pushes the seafloor apart, and cools into new basalt, so the ocean crust on either side of the ridge is constantly being renewed. The direct evidence for this process was gathered in the 1960s, when geologists mapped magnetic patterns on the seafloor and found that they mirror, in reverse, the record of reversals in Earth's magnetic field that has been recovered from land-based rock. Bands of rock with normal polarity and bands with reversed polarity alternate in symmetrical pairs on the two sides of the ridge, with the youngest, normal-polarity band running right along its crest. Since the 1960s, thousands of small earthquakes mapped along the ridge have confirmed that spreading is happening now, at a rate of roughly two centimeters per year in much of the mid-Atlantic.
question: What is the main topic of the passage?
options: The history of seafloor exploration along the mid-Atlantic ridge
Evidence that new ocean crust forms continuously at mid-ocean ridges
The effect of Earth's magnetic field on basalt cooling
The comparison between land-based rock and seafloor rock
explanation: 答案B。全段核心是“mountain building on the deep ocean floor... magma rises... cools into new basalt... ocean crust... constantly being renewed”，磁条带和地震是“direct evidence”和“confirmed”的新证据。A“历史”不是主题；C偏离，磁场只是证据材料；D比较只是支撑手段。

passage: When people estimate how fast a moving car is traveling, they do not measure its position over time in the way a speedometer does. Instead, experiments suggest that the brain builds the estimate from several noisy signals at once: the visual flow of the road surface, the sound the car makes, and a rough sense of how long the car has been in view. Each of these signals is imperfect on its own, but the brain appears to weight them according to their reliability in the current conditions. In bright daylight with the road clearly visible, visual flow carries most of the weight; in heavy rain, the sound of the engine may dominate. This weighting is not fixed: if a driver wears a hearing aid, people around him sometimes adjust their estimates to trust the visual signal more, as if the listener's own uncertainty were readable to others. Researchers are now studying whether the same balancing act underlies our judgments of human speed—that is, how fast a person is walking—where there is no road surface or engine noise to rely on.
question: The author mentions hearing aids primarily in order to
options: suggest that drivers should avoid wearing hearing aids when estimating speed
describe how hearing aids alter the sound of a car's engine
illustrate that the weighting of sensory signals can shift when one source becomes less trustworthy
argue that visual flow is the most reliable signal for judging speed
explanation: 答案C。作者先说明大脑“weight them according to their reliability”，随后举例：“if a driver wears a hearing aid, people around him sometimes adjust their estimates to trust the visual signal more”——当某个感觉来源可信度下降时权重随之调整。这正是为了展示权重可以变化。B以偏概全；C文中无建议；D偏离主题。

passage: The social scientist Turner T. Lamani has spent two decades studying how neighborhoods transform when large employers relocate. Her central finding is that the departure of a major employer does not immediately change the character of a neighborhood, but that the effects build up over generations through a process she calls “credential drift.” When a plant closes, the first response is usually economic: unemployment rises, businesses fail. But within a decade or two, Lamani observes, the pattern that matters most is which children from the affected families finish high school, finish college, or leave the neighborhood altogether. Families whose parents had jobs near the school tend to keep their children in local schools, while families whose parents work long commutes elsewhere are more likely to send their children to schools in other districts. Over time, the neighborhood's school population shifts from the children of long-time residents to the children of newer arrivals, and the cultural practices, expectations, and even the slang of the school change accordingly. Lamani argues that this drift is invisible in year-by-year statistics but decisive for the neighborhood's future.
question: According to the passage, what does “credential drift” refer to?
options: The immediate rise in unemployment after a plant closes
The gradual shift in a neighborhood's school population and associated cultural practices
The tendency of school districts to merge with neighboring districts
The increase in long commutes for workers after a factory relocates
explanation: 答案B。文中定义性句子：“the pattern that matters most is which children... finish high school... Over time, the neighborhood's school population shifts from the children of long-time residents to the children of newer arrivals, and the cultural practices, expectations, and even the slang of the school change accordingly.”这正是“credential drift”的含义。A是“first response”而非drift本身；C、D文中未提。

passage: "The human eye can detect the faintest bioluminescent display under the right conditions, but far more interesting are the deep-sea animals that make light deliberately to improve their own hunting. One such animal is the small, mostly blind goblin shark. Its eyes are simple light detectors, useless for forming images, yet it hunts by driving prey into a narrow pocket of water where the shark's own side flippers, which carry rows of specialized photophores, light up. The effect is not a steady lamp but a rapid, flickering wash of blue light, and experiments in which sharks were filmed with low-light sensors suggest that the flicker startles plankton and small crustaceans, causing them to scatter, which the shark then catches with a quick snap of its jaw. Researchers note that the photophores are maintained even in the dark of the deep ocean, where no daylight exists to make the shark a silhouette, hinting that the display serves no camouflage function whatsoever.
question: According to the passage, what role does the flickering blue light play in the goblin shark's hunting?
options: It startles small prey, causing them to scatter
It camouflages the shark against the dark background
It attracts larger predators away from the shark
It helps the shark form images of its surroundings
explanation: 答案A。文中写道：“experiments... suggest that the flicker startles plankton and small crustaceans, causing them to scatter, which the shark then catches with a quick snap of its jaw.”B与最后一段“hinting that the display serves no camouflage function whatsoever”矛盾；C、D文中未提，D与“simple light detectors, useless for forming images”不符。

passage: In 1947, the economist Richard Arnold proposed a model of how wages are set in a competitive labor market with asymmetric information. The central assumption is that a firm can observe an individual worker's output after hiring, but it cannot perfectly observe the worker's effort, because some types of work involve unobservable judgment calls. Under these conditions, Arnold argued, firms will offer contracts that include a fixed base salary plus a bonus tied to output, because the bonus component aligns the worker's incentives with the firm's interests. However, the model also predicts a trade-off: the greater the bonus, the more volatile the worker's total income becomes, and risk-averse workers will demand a higher base salary to accept a riskier bonus structure. Arnold noted that in practice, highly skilled workers often negotiate flat salaries rather than bonus-laden contracts, while less-skilled workers in routine jobs accept a larger share of their pay in bonuses. This asymmetry, he suggested, may help explain why compensation structures differ so widely across industries.
question: It can be inferred from the passage that, under Arnold's model, a risk-averse worker offered a contract with a very large bonus component would most likely
options: accept the contract without any adjustment to the base salary
request a reduction in the bonus to make the contract more attractive
demand a higher base salary in exchange for accepting the bonus
prefer a contract with no bonus at all
explanation: 答案C。文中写道：“the greater the bonus, the more volatile the worker's total income becomes, and risk-averse workers will demand a higher base salary to accept a riskier bonus structure.”风险厌恶型工人面对更大奖金（更大波动）时会要求提高基本工资，C直接对应。A与模型矛盾；B方向相反；D“no bonus at all”超出模型预测范围。

passage: The practice of painting with cadmium yellow, a pigment made from cadmium sulfide, introduced a new problem for painters in the nineteenth century: the pigment is chemically stable in its dry state, but it reacts with the linseed oil that forms the binding medium in oil paint. The reaction is slow, but it is not reversible, and over decades the yellow darkens into an olive green that no amount of restoration can fully correct. Several painters of the late nineteenth century were aware of this tendency, and correspondence among them reveals a shared strategy: they used cadmium yellow sparingly, reserving it for accents, and mixed it with other pigments in ways that reduced the proportion of cadmium sulfide in any single brushstroke. The painter Isidore Vellum, in a letter to a colleague, described the effect as “a slow, quiet betrayal that takes forty years to announce itself.” Vellum's approach, according to art conservators, was more rigorous than that of his contemporaries; his paintings, executed with cadmium yellow restricted to thin, well-bound layers, have largely retained their original color.
question: The word “it” in the sentence “The reaction is slow, but it is not reversible” refers to
options: the reaction between cadmium sulfide and linseed oil
explanation: 答案C。前一句说“the pigment is chemically stable in its dry state, but it reacts with the linseed oil”，紧接着说“The reaction is slow, but it is not reversible”。代词“it”指代的是上一句中已经提到的“the reaction”，即镉硫化物与亚麻籽油之间的化学反应。A、B是反应物，D是反应的后果而非反应本身。

passage: For most of the twelfth century, the Mediterranean trade network operated under a set of customs that had evolved over generations: merchants paid a fixed share of their cargo's value to the port authority, disputes were settled by a council of senior merchants, and the physical movement of goods was governed by a series of local agreements that gave each port a defined role. The arrival of the Crusader states in the early 1100s disrupted this system in a way that historians continue to debate. Some scholars emphasize the military angle: the Crusader knights needed to be supplied from Italy and were therefore a new, powerful class of customers whose demands reshaped the terms of trade. Others stress the commercial angle: the Crusader states themselves became trading partners, issuing their own coinage and establishing customs arrangements that directly competed with those of the established ports. A third view, advanced by the economic historian Marta Osei, focuses on the redistribution of risk: because the Crusader campaigns made certain routes more dangerous, merchants began to consolidate their cargo in larger, better-armed vessels, which favored the wealthier merchants and gradually excluded smaller operators from the most profitable routes.
question: What is the main point of the passage?
options: The Crusader states issued their own coinage, which weakened the established ports' authority.
The Crusader campaigns led to the complete collapse of Mediterranean trade customs.
Historians disagree about which factors most significantly disrupted twelfth-century Mediterranean trade.
Marta Osei's view is the most widely accepted explanation among economic historians.
explanation: 答案C。全段结构为：背景→“in a way that historians continue to debate”→三种不同观点（military angle / commercial angle / Osei's risk angle），C准确概括了“史学家对影响因素存在分歧”这一主旨。A只涉及第二种观点的一部分；B“complete collapse”过度；D文中未给出接受度判断。

passage: Volcanic activity beneath the Earth's ocean floor creates a surprisingly diverse range of rock types, and the mineral assemblage found in any given basalt sample can serve as a fingerprint for the conditions under which the magma formed. One key indicator is the presence of a mineral called olivine: when olivine is abundant in a basalt, it tells geologists that the magma was drawn from a relatively deep part of the mantle and was not heavily modified as it rose through the crust. A second indicator is the ratio of potassium to sodium, a ratio that shifts in a predictable direction as magma passes through older, potassium-rich crustal rocks. By combining these two measurements, geologists can reconstruct a broad outline of the plumbing system that carried the magma from the mantle to the surface. Recent work on mid-ocean ridge basalts has refined this approach further, revealing that the potassium-to-sodium ratio varies systematically along the length of the ridge, a pattern that researchers interpret as reflecting differences in the temperature of the underlying mantle at different locations.
question: As used in the passage, the word “fingerprint” most nearly means
explanation: 答案B。文中说“the mineral assemblage found in any given basalt sample can serve as a fingerprint for the conditions under which the magma formed”，即矿物组合能够像指纹一样识别岩浆形成的条件，fingerprint 在此比喻“独特的识别特征”。A（污染标记）、C（生物残留物）、D（装饰图案）均不符合语境。

passage: In the 1980s, the developmental psychologist Karen Mott introduced a simple experimental setup that became a standard tool in the field: two identical boxes, one containing a small light and one containing a small bell, and a young child who had been told to press a button to hear the bell. Mott's design was deliberately simple, and her reasoning was that complexity in the setup would obscure the very phenomenon she wanted to measure—namely, whether children form a causal expectation that pressing the button will produce the bell, or whether they merely form a spatial association between the button and the box that happens to contain the bell. By using two boxes that looked identical, Mott eliminated spatial cues that might allow children to guess which box was “correct” without understanding the causal link. The experiments that followed confirmed her hypothesis: children as young as three formed a genuine causal expectation, and their behavior changed predictably when the causal link was broken—for example, when the bell rang without the button being pressed, the children looked at the button, not at the box.
question: The author mentions that the two boxes were identical primarily in order to
options: explain why Mott chose a bell rather than a light as the signal
show that spatial cues were eliminated, so the causal link could be tested independently
argue that identical objects are more engaging for young children
suggest that Mott's experiments were poorly designed
explanation: 答案B。文中写道：“By using two boxes that looked identical, Mott eliminated spatial cues that might allow children to guess which box was 'correct' without understanding the causal link.”这正是提及箱子相同的原因——排除空间线索，独立检验因果联系。A（为什么选铃铛）文中未解释；C（更有趣）无依据；D（设计缺陷）与原文意图相反。

passage: The sociologist Lena Fischer has studied how urban residents form what she calls “neighborhood identity,” a sense of belonging to a place that is not defined by official boundaries but by shared experience of specific streets, shops, and public spaces. Fischer's surveys, conducted in three European cities over a period of ten years, found that neighborhood identity is strongest not in areas with the highest residential stability but in areas that have experienced a moderate degree of change: new residents have arrived, but long-time residents remain, and the two groups interact daily in local markets and schools. In areas where change has been dramatic—where entire blocks have been demolished and rebuilt—neighborhood identity is weakest, because the shared reference points that residents use to orient themselves in their daily lives have been physically erased. Fischer argues that the finding has implications for urban planning: rather than trying to freeze neighborhoods in their current form, planners should aim for a pace of change that allows new residents to build their own reference points without completely displacing the existing ones.
question: According to the passage, in which type of area is neighborhood identity weakest?
options: An area with a moderate degree of change and active local markets
An area with the highest residential stability
An area where new residents and long-time residents interact daily
An area where entire blocks have been demolished and rebuilt
explanation: 答案D。文中明确指出：“In areas where change has been dramatic—where entire blocks have been demolished and rebuilt—neighborhood identity is weakest, because the shared reference points... have been physically erased.”A与B与“strongest”条件相关；B是“moderate degree of change”，对应identity strongest。

passage: The intestinal microbiome—the community of trillions of bacteria living in the human gut—has long been dismissed by mainstream medicine as a minor curiosity. That attitude changed in the early 2000s, when a series of studies found that individuals with irritable bowel syndrome had measurably different bacterial populations than healthy controls. The discovery opened a new line of research, and within a decade, studies linking specific gut bacteria to conditions as diverse as depression, type 2 diabetes, and autoimmune disorders had accumulated to the point where the field could no longer be ignored. The mechanism by which gut bacteria influence distant organs is not fully understood, but one leading hypothesis centers on a short-chain fatty acid called butyrate, which gut bacteria produce when they ferment dietary fiber. Butyrate is absorbed by the intestinal wall and enters the bloodstream, where it may modulate immune signaling in the gut and, through yet-unknown pathways, in other tissues. Researchers emphasize that correlation does not yet establish causation, but the pace of clinical trials testing direct manipulation of the microbiome suggests that the field is moving quickly from observation to intervention.
question: Which of the following best captures the central point of the passage?
options: Butyrate is the only compound produced by gut bacteria that affects human health.
The gut microbiome is too diverse for any meaningful medical research to be conducted.
Research into the gut microbiome has shifted from dismissal to active investigation and clinical trials.
Irritable bowel syndrome is the only condition linked to gut bacteria.
explanation: 答案C。全段讲述从“dismissed as a minor curiosity”到“opened a new line of research”再到“moving quickly from observation to intervention”的转变，C准确概括了这一下行弧线。A“only”过度；B与原文意图相反；D“only condition”与“as diverse as depression, type 2 diabetes, and autoimmune disorders”矛盾。

passage: The Hubble Space Telescope, launched in 1990, was designed with a primary mirror that was slightly misshapen—a defect caused by a small error in the polishing process. The result was that images taken with the full mirror were blurry, with light from a point source spread across a halo instead of concentrating in a sharp spot. The flaw was diagnosed within months, and engineers designed a corrective optical device called COSTAR, which was installed during a space shuttle repair mission in 1993. COSTAR worked by introducing a precisely calculated opposite distortion, effectively canceling out the mirror's error. After the repair, Hubble's image quality exceeded the specifications of many ground-based telescopes that had not yet been built. In subsequent years, each of Hubble's major instruments was designed to be self-correcting, so that the lessons of the COSTAR repair did not need to be repeated. The telescope has now been operational for over three decades, and its scientific output remains among the highest of any space observatory ever launched.
question: It can be inferred from the passage that before the COSTAR repair, Hubble's images of point sources
options: were completely unusable for scientific purposes
showed light spread in a halo rather than a sharp concentration
were sharper than those produced by any ground-based telescope
were not affected by the mirror defect because Hubble used a different optical path
explanation: 答案B。文中写道：“The result was that images taken with the full mirror were blurry, with light from a point source spread across a halo instead of concentrating in a sharp spot.”B直接复述该事实。A“completely unusable”过度；C方向相反，COSTAR后才“exceeded the specifications of many ground-based telescopes”；D与原文直接矛盾。

passage: The construction of the Pantheon in Rome, completed around 125 CE, remains one of the most technically ambitious achievements of the ancient world. Its dome, which spans 43 meters, is the largest unreinforced concrete dome ever built, and the engineering problems it posed were severe. The weight of the dome alone would have exerted enormous lateral thrust on the supporting walls, a force that in ordinary construction would cause the walls to bulge outward and eventually collapse. The Roman engineers addressed this problem through several means: they used a concrete mixture whose aggregate varied with height, with heavy basalt stones at the base and much lighter pumice near the top; they embedded iron clamps in the concrete to reinforce the joints; and they designed a series of coffered panels in the ceiling of the dome, which reduced the total weight while adding decorative relief. A further element, the oculus—a circular opening at the apex of the dome that was never covered—reduced the weight of the very top of the structure and admitted a single column of light that has been a defining feature of the building's interior since its completion.
question: As used in the passage, the word “coffered” most nearly means
options: hollowed out in a decorative pattern
covered with a thin layer of plaster
explanation: 答案C。文中说“they designed a series of coffered panels in the ceiling of the dome, which reduced the total weight while adding decorative relief”。coffered 指的是凹入的格状装饰板，即表面有凹陷格纹的面板，既减轻重量又增加装饰效果。A（彩色）B（铁条）D（石膏层）均不符合“reduced the total weight”的描述。

passage: The concept of “creative destruction,” coined by the economist Joseph Schumpeter in the 1940s, describes a process by which new technologies render older industries obsolete, destroying existing jobs and businesses while creating new ones. Schumpeter argued that this process is not a disruption to be corrected but the fundamental mechanism of economic progress. In his model, a firm that introduces a superior technology earns a temporary monopoly profit, which attracts competitors, which in turn erodes the monopoly, and the cycle repeats. The important implication is that the destruction and the creation are linked: the firms that are destroyed free up resources—labor, capital, and entrepreneurial talent—that are then absorbed by the new industries. Schumpeter was aware that the process could be painful for individuals, and he acknowledged that policy could ease the transition. But he argued that any policy that tried to prevent the destruction would ultimately slow the creation and reduce the long-run gains from technological change. Modern economists generally accept his core insight while disagreeing about how quickly resources are reallocated and whether the transition costs are properly distributed across the population.
question: According to the passage, Schumpeter believed that resources freed up by destroyed firms would
options: remain unused until the government intervened
be destroyed along with the firms
explanation: 答案B。文中写道：“The firms that are destroyed free up resources—labor, capital, and entrepreneurial talent—that are then absorbed by the new industries.”B直接复述该结论。A（需政府干预）与“any policy that tried to prevent the destruction”相矛盾；C（资源也被摧毁）与“free up”矛盾；D（被竞争对手囤积）文中未提。

passage: Coral reefs are typically thought of as warm-water ecosystems, but some corals live in cold, deep water where sunlight does not reach. These so-called cold-water corals, which belong to a different group of species from the familiar tropical corals, grow very slowly—some individuals are estimated to be more than nine hundred years old. Because they lack the symbiotic algae that tropical corals host, cold-water corals do not need sunlight to survive; instead, they feed on drifting plankton and organic particles that sink from above. Their slow growth rate means that a single colony can take centuries to build the dense, branching structure that makes a cold-water reef recognizable on the seafloor. The implications of this slow growth are significant for conservation: damage caused by deep-sea trawling, which can scrape the seabed and break coral branches, takes decades to centuries to recover, if it recovers at all. For this reason, several oceanic regions now include cold-water coral formations in their protected areas, and the mapping of these formations has become a priority for marine resource managers who are trying to balance fishing interests against long-term ecological stability.
question: The word “they” in the passage most nearly refers to
explanation: 答案C。定位句：“Because they lack the symbiotic algae that tropical corals host, cold-water corals do not need sunlight to survive.”代词“they”的主语是前一句的主语“cold-water corals”，即冷水珊瑚缺乏热带珊瑚所具有的共生藻类，因此不需要阳光。A（热带珊瑚）是后接定语从句的主语；B（藻类）是缺少之物；D（浮游生物）是食物来源，均非指代对象。

passage: Among the most celebrated examples of evolutionary adaptation is Batesian mimicry, in which a palatable species evolves to resemble a distasteful or poisonous species, thereby gaining protection from predators that have learned to avoid the model. The classic case involves butterflies of the genus Papilio, several species of which mimic the toxic swallowtails of the genus Battus. What makes the system particularly instructive is not the resemblance itself but its fine-grained control: in some populations, only the females are mimics, while males retain the ancestral, non-mimetic pattern. Field observations suggest that this difference reflects the differing costs of being eaten: females, which must survive long enough to lay eggs, benefit more from the protection than males, whose reproductive success depends less on prolonged survival. Researchers have also documented geographic variation in the fidelity of the mimicry: in regions where the toxic model is abundant, the imitations are strikingly precise, whereas in areas where the model is scarce, the resemblance degrades noticeably.
question: According to the passage, in which regions is the butterflies' mimicry the most precise?
options: Regions where the resident butterfly populations are largest
Regions where the females do not mimic the toxic model
Regions where the toxic model species is abundant
Regions where predators have stopped hunting butterflies altogether
explanation: 答案C。文中明确写道“in regions where the toxic model is abundant, the imitations are strikingly precise, whereas in areas where the model is scarce, the resemblance degrades noticeably”，即在有毒模式种丰富的地区，模仿最精确；模式种稀少时模仿质量明显下降。A、B、D 文中均无依据。

passage: Desert pavements—the smooth, tightly packed layers of pebbles that cover large stretches of arid land—have long puzzled geologists, because the processes that create them are not obvious from the surface alone. The pavement appears to rest directly on the soil, but excavations reveal a different structure: beneath the pebbles lies a layer of fine silt, and beneath that, in many cases, a crust of calcium carbonate hardened over millennia. For years the standard explanation was wind erosion: the idea being that the wind gradually removed the fine particles between the stones, leaving the larger fragments behind as a lag deposit. More recent experiments, however, suggest that the pavement is not simply what is left over after erosion. Instead, dust falling from the atmosphere accumulates beneath the stones—trapped by the pebbles and worked downward by the swelling and shrinking of the soil with each rain—so that the pavement is actually built up from below while the exposed surface stays level. The two mechanisms are not mutually exclusive, but their relative importance varies from one desert to another.
question: What does the passage mainly discuss about desert pavements?
options: Wind erosion has been conclusively shown to play no role in the formation of desert pavements
The formation of desert pavements involves competing explanations, with recent research emphasizing buildup from below rather than simple wind erosion
Desert pavements develop only in regions that receive heavy rainfall each year
Calcium carbonate crusts beneath the pavement are the direct cause of the smooth surface on top
explanation: 答案B。全段先介绍传统解释“the standard explanation was wind erosion”，再提出新证据“the pavement is actually built up from below”，并总结“The two mechanisms are not mutually exclusive”，B概括了两种解释并存、新研究强调自下而上堆积的主旨。A“no role whatsoever”过度否定；C与“arid land”矛盾；D颠倒因果，文中钙壳只是地层之一。

passage: Venus, the second planet from the Sun, is often called Earth's twin because of its similar size and mass, yet its surface conditions are so extreme that the comparison quickly breaks down. The planet is wrapped in a dense atmosphere of carbon dioxide that traps heat with extraordinary efficiency, producing a surface temperature of roughly 460 degrees Celsius—hot enough to melt lead. Compounding the heat is the atmospheric pressure, which at the surface is about ninety times that of Earth, a crushing weight equivalent to being nearly a kilometer underwater. The atmosphere also carries clouds of sulfuric acid, whose caustic droplets drift through the upper air and occasionally condense into rain that evaporates long before reaching the ground. Radar mapping has revealed that the surface itself is remarkably young, dominated by volcanic plains and few impact craters, suggesting that large-scale resurfacing events have erased most of the planet's early history. Because of these conditions, the Soviet probes that landed in the 1970s survived for barely an hour before their electronics failed, a testament to the hostility of the environment.
question: As used in the passage, the word “caustic” most nearly means
explanation: 答案A。语境为“clouds of sulfuric acid, whose caustic droplets drift through the upper air”，硫酸液滴对设备具有腐蚀性，且后文说苏联探测器“survived for barely an hour before their electronics failed”，印证 caustic 意为“腐蚀性的”，与 corrosive 同义。harmless（无害）、diluted（稀释）、transparent（透明）均不符。

passage: Studies of memory consolidation have repeatedly pointed to sleep as a critical period during which the brain transforms fragile new memories into stable, long-term ones. In one widely replicated experiment, participants who learned a list of word pairs and then slept for eight hours recalled significantly more the next morning than participants who stayed awake for the same period, even though both groups spent the same total time on the task. The effect was especially pronounced for emotionally charged material, which suggests that the sleeping brain prioritizes information with survival value. Neuroimaging during sleep has revealed patterns of brain activity that mirror the patterns produced during learning, as if the daytime experience were being replayed at an accelerated rate. Researchers differ, however, on the question of whether this replay is a faithful reproduction of what was learned or a selective editing of it. Some argue that the brain strengthens the original traces wholesale; others maintain that it actively discards competing details, and that the remembered version diverges from the original experience in systematic ways.
question: It can be inferred from the passage that the author would most likely agree that
options: staying awake for eight hours improves recall more effectively than sleeping
the brain's replay of daytime experiences during sleep may alter some details of what was learned
sleep serves primarily to strengthen memories that carry no emotional weight
researchers now agree that sleep reproduces learned material with complete fidelity
explanation: 答案B。文中指出研究者对重放是“a faithful reproduction”还是“a selective editing”存在分歧，并说“others maintain that it actively discards competing details, and that the remembered version diverges from the original experience”，由此可推断睡眠中的重放可能改变所学内容的某些细节。A与“emotionally charged material”效果更明显矛盾；B与“Researchers differ”矛盾；C与实验结论相反。

passage: A persistent myth in economics textbooks is that money evolved to solve the inefficiencies of barter: a farmer with surplus wheat who wants fish must find a fisherman who wants wheat, a coincidence of wants that is rare enough to make direct exchange impractical. The story is tidy, and it appears in countless introductory chapters, but anthropologists who study actual exchange in small-scale societies have found little evidence that pure barter ever dominated daily life. Among the peoples of highland New Guinea, for example, elaborate systems of gift exchange operate according to social rules in which the value of an object depends less on what it is than on the history of the relationship between the people exchanging it. Historians of money point out that the earliest known currencies—cowrie shells, barley, cattle—functioned primarily as units of account and as means of storing value for tribute and compensation, roles that are poorly served by the ad hoc swapping that the textbook story describes. The barter myth persists, these scholars argue, because it offers a conveniently simple origin story, not because the archaeological record supports it.
question: Why does the author mention the peoples of highland New Guinea?
options: To provide evidence that exchange in small-scale societies was governed by social rules rather than pure barter
To show that gift exchange is more efficient than the use of money
To argue that money originated in the highlands of New Guinea
To illustrate the coincidence of wants problem in daily practice
explanation: 答案A。该例子出现在“anthropologists... have found little evidence that pure barter ever dominated daily life”之后，用“for example”引出：“elaborate systems of gift exchange operate according to social rules”，说明小规模社会中的交换由社会规则支配而非纯粹物物交换。B、C 文中未提；D与例子意图相反。

passage: Paper currency was invented in China during the Song dynasty, but its rise was driven less by economic theory than by a practical crisis. In the eleventh century, the government faced a chronic shortage of the copper coins that served as the standard medium of exchange, in part because the state itself was melting coins down to cast bronze statues and because merchants were hoarding the metal. The government's first response was to experiment with iron coins, but these proved so heavy that a single large purchase required a wheelbarrow. Private merchants in the city of Chengdu, in the western province of Sichuan, then began issuing their own notes—receipts that could be redeemed for iron coins at the issuer's shop. The experiment succeeded, and the state soon took control of the system, standardizing the size of the notes, mandating a reserve of metal to back them, and fixing the exchange rate. As the notes circulated, however, governments repeatedly printed more of them than the reserves justified, and the resulting inflation reminded later dynasties of the dangers of unbacked currency, a lesson that would be relearned centuries later in Europe.
question: According to the passage, what was one of the causes of the shortage of copper coins during the Song dynasty?
options: Merchants in Chengdu refused to accept copper coins in payment
Iron coins replaced copper coins throughout the entire empire
The government itself melted coins down to cast bronze statues
The state mandated that a reserve of metal must back every note
explanation: 答案C。原文明确列出铜钱短缺的原因：“in part because the state itself was melting coins down to cast bronze statues and because merchants were hoarding the metal”。A、B 文中未提（铁钱只是试点，并未全国取代）；D是后来的纸币准备金制度，与短缺原因无关。

passage: When the painter Claude Monet exhibited a canvas titled Impression, Sunrise in 1874, he could not have anticipated that a critic's dismissive pun would give a movement its name. The loose brushwork and emphasis on the play of light that characterized the painting were, to the critic, evidence of sloppy technique, mere impressions rather than finished works. The label stuck, and the artists who had shown together that spring—Monet, Renoir, Sisley, and others—adopted it as a badge of honor. Their shared project was not a common style in the strict sense but a common set of procedures: painting out of doors rather than in the studio, working quickly to capture a moment of light before it changed, and rejecting the dark, carefully glazed surfaces favored by the academic establishment. The new methods demanded new materials, and the invention of collapsible paint tubes, which allowed pigments to be carried easily into the field, is often cited as a precondition for the movement. What unified the group, in the end, was less a doctrine than a conviction that the eye, not the studio's conventions, should dictate what the painter recorded.
question: The word “Their” in the passage refers to
options: Monet and the other artists who exhibited together in 1874
the inventors of collapsible paint tubes
explanation: 答案B。定位句：“The label stuck, and the artists who had shown together that spring—Monet, Renoir, Sisley, and others—adopted it as a badge of honor. Their shared project was...” ，“Their”指代紧邻前句的主语“the artists who had shown together that spring”，即与莫奈一同参展的画家群体。A（评论家）、C（学院派）、D（颜料管发明者）均非指代对象。

passage: Urban economists have long debated whether the process of gentrification—the influx of wealthier residents into previously working-class neighborhoods—benefits or harms the original inhabitants. The evidence, it turns out, is mixed and depends heavily on what one measures. Studies that track property values find that homes in gentrifying districts appreciate faster than those in comparable non-gentrifying areas, which benefits owners but can squeeze renters, whose rents rise without any corresponding gain in equity. Studies that track employment find that gentrification is associated with a modest increase in local jobs, but almost all of the new positions are in retail, food service, and construction, industries that do not necessarily employ the existing residents. One of the most robust findings, however, concerns displacement: contrary to popular belief, poor households in gentrifying neighborhoods move out at rates only slightly higher than those in non-gentrifying neighborhoods, though those who do move tend to relocate to poorer, more disadvantaged areas. The researchers caution that averages conceal wide variation, and that city-level policies can substantially change the outcome for any given neighborhood.
question: According to the passage, which of the following is one of the most robust findings about gentrification?
options: The new jobs created by gentrification go mainly to long-term residents
Rents in gentrifying districts rise more slowly than property values
Poor households in gentrifying neighborhoods move out at rates only slightly higher than those in other neighborhoods
Gentrification causes most poor households to relocate to wealthier districts
explanation: 答案C。原文写道“One of the most robust findings, however, concerns displacement: contrary to popular belief, poor households in gentrifying neighborhoods move out at rates only slightly higher than those in non-gentrifying neighborhoods”。B与“relocate to poorer, more disadvantaged areas”相反；C与“do not necessarily employ the existing residents”矛盾；D与“rents rise”趋势相反。

passage: Anyone who has stepped from a city park onto an asphalt street on a summer afternoon has felt the urban heat island effect: the tendency of built-up areas to be warmer than the surrounding countryside. The effect arises from a combination of factors. Dark roofs and pavement absorb solar radiation and re-emit it slowly as heat; buildings and roads replace vegetation that would otherwise cool the air through evaporation; and the waste heat from vehicles and air conditioners adds energy directly to the urban atmosphere. The temperature difference between a large city and its rural hinterland can reach several degrees, and it is most pronounced at night, when the stored heat of the day is released while the countryside cools rapidly. The consequences are not merely uncomfortable. Heat waves kill more people in cities than in the countryside, the demand for air conditioning drives up energy consumption in a vicious cycle, and the warmer nights exacerbate air pollution by trapping pollutants near the ground. Urban planners have responded with a range of measures, from planting street trees and building green roofs to mandating reflective coatings on new construction.
question: The passage is primarily concerned with which of the following aspects of the urban heat island effect?
options: Air conditioning is the single largest cause of urban warming
Cities are warmer at night because they consume more energy during the day
Planting street trees has eliminated the urban heat island effect in most large cities
The urban heat island effect results from several interacting causes and has significant practical consequences
explanation: 答案D。全段结构为“arises from a combination of factors”（多种因素）加“The consequences are not merely uncomfortable”（实际后果严重），最后以应对措施收尾，D全面概括。A以偏概全（空调只是因素之一）；B因果颠倒（夜间更暖源于白天储存的热量释放）；C“eliminated”与“responded with a range of measures”矛盾。

passage: The sinking of coastal land, a process geologists call subsidence, is a growing hazard in several of the world's largest port cities. In many cases the cause is not geology but human activity: the extraction of groundwater for drinking and irrigation removes the water that once supported the underground sediments, allowing the ground to compact and settle. Measurements from satellite radar show that some districts in Jakarta, Ho Chi Minh City, and Shanghai are sinking by several centimeters per year, a rate that far outpaces the few millimeters of sea-level rise attributed to climate change. The combination is doubly dangerous, because subsidence increases the depth of floodwaters when storms arrive and permanently reduces the elevation of the land relative to the sea. Engineers have proposed a range of remedies, from injecting water back into depleted aquifers to building massive sea walls, but the most effective single measure is simpler: reducing the amount of groundwater extracted in the first place. Cities that have restricted pumping, such as Tokyo, have seen the rate of subsidence slow dramatically.
question: As used in the passage, the word “subsidence” most nearly means
options: a gradual sinking of the ground
a rapid rise in sea level
explanation: 答案B。文章开头即定义“The sinking of coastal land, a process geologists call subsidence”，并且后文说地下水被抽出后“allowing the ground to compact and settle”，城市正“sinking by several centimeters per year”，可见 subsidence 意为“地面缓慢下沉”。A（建筑突然倒塌）、C（地下水压力增大）、D（海平面上升，文中是与下沉对比的另一个过程）均不符。

passage: The archaeological site of Göbekli Tepe, in southeastern Turkey, has forced a rethinking of the standard narrative of how complex societies began. The site consists of a series of circular enclosures ringed by massive limestone pillars, some weighing more than ten tons, carved with images of foxes, birds, and other animals. Radiocarbon dating places the earliest structures at roughly 11,500 years ago, which is to say they were built before the invention of pottery, before metallurgy, and—critically—before the domestication of wheat, at a time when the people of the region were still hunter-gatherers. The standard assumption had been that large-scale monumental construction required settled farming communities with surplus food to support the builders. At Göbekli Tepe, however, the monuments appear to have come first: the settlement and the agricultural practices that later surrounded it seem to have grown up around the site, not to have preceded it. Excavators have found evidence that the enclosures were deliberately backfilled at the end of their use, their pillars toppled and buried in a single event, as if the builders were sealing the site away on purpose.
question: It can be inferred from the passage that the construction of Göbekli Tepe challenges the assumption that
options: monumental building required settled farming communities with surplus food
hunter-gatherers were incapable of carving images of animals
circular enclosures were used primarily for the burial of the dead
the site was built after the invention of pottery and metallurgy
explanation: 答案A。文中先给出旧假设：“The standard assumption had been that large-scale monumental construction required settled farming communities with surplus food”，随后用“At Göbekli Tepe, however, the monuments appear to have come first”直接反驳，说明该遗址的建造先于农耕定居，挑战的正是A中的假设。B、C文中未提；D与文中“built before the invention of pottery”矛盾。

passage: The oceans do not simply sit in place; they circulate in a global pattern driven by differences in temperature and salinity, a system known as the thermohaline circulation. In the North Atlantic, warm surface water carried northward from the tropics loses heat to the cold air above it and also loses fresh water through evaporation. As the water cools and becomes saltier, it grows denser, and eventually it sinks in a process called deep-water formation, plunging thousands of meters to the ocean floor. From there, the dense water spreads southward and eastward, flows around the southern tip of Africa, and enters the Indian and Pacific Oceans, where it slowly rises again after being warmed and diluted over centuries. The circulation matters far beyond the oceans themselves: it transports enormous quantities of heat toward the poles, moderating the climate of western Europe, and it carries dissolved oxygen into the deep sea, sustaining the ecosystems that live there. Paleoclimatologists have found evidence that the circulation has stalled repeatedly in the past, most dramatically during the last ice age, when the injection of huge volumes of fresh meltwater into the North Atlantic appears to have shut it down.
question: According to the passage, what initiates the sinking of surface water in the North Atlantic?
options: Dissolved oxygen is consumed by deep-sea ecosystems, lightening the water
The water is warmed by tropical sunlight and expands as a result
Fresh meltwater from melting ice sheets floods into the region
The water cools and becomes saltier, growing denser than the water beneath it
explanation: 答案D。原文写道“As the water cools and becomes saltier, it grows denser, and eventually it sinks in a process called deep-water formation”，即变冷、变咸导致密度增大而下沉。A方向相反（增温膨胀会减轻密度）；B描述的是冰期使环流停滞的事件，而非下沉的起因；D文中未提。

passage: The placebo effect—the measurable improvement in a patient's condition that follows the administration of an inert treatment—has been documented so often that it is sometimes treated as a nuisance to be controlled for in clinical trials. But a growing number of researchers argue that the effect is not a nuisance at all but a genuine phenomenon worthy of study in its own right. Brain-imaging studies have shown that placebo treatments can trigger the release of endorphins, the brain's own painkillers, in the same regions activated by morphine. The size of the effect varies with context: injections produce larger placebo responses than pills, and branded medications produce larger responses than generic ones, suggesting that the patient's expectations are shaped by the rituals of medicine as much as by the chemistry. Some researchers have even demonstrated the effect in reverse, showing that telling patients honestly that they are receiving a placebo does not eliminate the response entirely, provided the explanation is framed in a way that preserves hope. The practical implication, these scientists contend, is not that doctors should deceive patients, but that the therapeutic encounter itself—attention, explanation, reassurance—is part of the treatment.
question: Why does the author mention that injections produce larger placebo responses than pills?
options: To illustrate that the placebo effect is shaped by the patient's expectations and the rituals of treatment
To argue that pills are ineffective forms of medication
To prove that the placebo effect is purely psychological and has no physical basis
To suggest that doctors should prefer injections for all treatments
explanation: 答案A。该例证位于“The size of the effect varies with context”之后，其结论是“the patient's expectations are shaped by the rituals of medicine as much as by the chemistry”，即治疗仪式影响期望、进而影响安慰剂效应的大小。B、C、D 均为对文意的曲解或过度引申。

passage: For most of recorded history, astronomers could only speculate about whether other stars possessed planets. That changed in 1995, with the discovery of a planet orbiting the star 51 Pegasi, and the field has since grown so rapidly that thousands of exoplanets are now catalogued. The earliest detections relied on the wobble method, which measures the slight gravitational tug a planet exerts on its star, visible as a periodic shift in the star's spectral lines. The method is biased toward massive planets in close orbits, which produce the largest wobbles, and this bias explains why the first planets found were so-called hot Jupiters, gas giants orbiting their stars in a matter of days. A second technique, the transit method, watches for the tiny dimming that occurs when a planet passes in front of its star; space observatories using this method have found most of the known exoplanets and have revealed that rocky planets in the habitable zone—the region where liquid water could exist—are surprisingly common. Each method has blind spots, and the best current estimates of a planet's properties combine data from several techniques.
question: Which of the following best summarizes the passage's account of how astronomers detect exoplanets?
options: The discovery of a planet orbiting 51 Pegasi and its unusual atmosphere
The techniques astronomers use to detect planets around other stars and the biases of each method
The reasons why planets in the habitable zone are rare in the galaxy
The history of the search for life beyond the solar system
explanation: 答案B。全段介绍两种探测方法（wobble method 和 transit method）及其各自偏向（“biased toward massive planets”“Each method has blind spots”），B准确概括。A只是引子；C与“surprisingly common”相反；D“搜寻地外生命”超出了段落范围。

passage: Few questions in labor economics have generated as much empirical work as the effect of minimum wage laws on employment. The theoretical prediction is straightforward: if the wage is set above the market-clearing level, employers will hire fewer workers. Yet the evidence from actual policy changes is far less clear. The most famous study, which compared fast-food restaurants on either side of a state border after one state raised its minimum wage, found no measurable reduction in employment, a result that surprised economists on both sides of the debate. Critics noted that the comparison was limited to one industry and one time period, and subsequent studies using different data have produced conflicting results. What has emerged from the accumulated research is a pattern best described as a consensus of uncertainty: most studies find small or negligible employment effects, but almost none can rule out modest negative effects for specific groups, particularly teenagers and low-skilled workers in regions with already weak labor markets. The scholarly debate continues, in part because the question is genuinely hard to answer with observational data: wages and employment move together for many reasons beyond the law itself.
question: It can be inferred from the passage that the border-state study of fast-food restaurants
options: provided evidence that a minimum wage increase did not necessarily reduce employment
was based on data from many different industries over several decades
proved that minimum wage laws always increase teenage unemployment
was rejected by every subsequent study in the field
explanation: 答案A。文中说该研究“found no measurable reduction in employment, a result that surprised economists on both sides of the debate”，即提高最低工资后就业并未可测下降，为A的推断提供直接依据。B与“limited to one industry and one time period”矛盾；C过于绝对且与结果不符；D与“subsequent studies... produced conflicting results”不符。

passage: The introduction of movable type in fifteenth-century Europe is usually credited with transforming European society, but the transformation was slower and more uneven than the popular account suggests. Gutenberg's invention, perfected around 1450, made it possible to produce identical copies of a text far more quickly than hand copying, yet for decades the new presses were used primarily to reproduce the same books that scribes had always copied: Bibles, devotional works, and legal texts. The number of books in circulation did multiply, but literacy rates rose only gradually, and printed books long remained expensive luxuries. What did change quickly was the geography of knowledge: a book printed in Venice could be shipped to London and sold there in the same year, and scholars across Europe could finally argue about the same text, page by page, instead of about variant handwritten copies. Later decades brought the features usually associated with print—cheap pamphlets, vernacular translations, and the rapid spread of new ideas—but these followed from the growth of a market for books as much as from the technology itself.
question: According to the passage, what did printed books make possible that handwritten copies had not?
options: Printed books became affordable for every household within a decade
Scholars in different countries could compare the same text page by page instead of variant handwritten copies
Literacy rates rose overnight throughout Europe
Scribes immediately abandoned the copying of devotional and legal texts
explanation: 答案B。原文写道“scholars across Europe could finally argue about the same text, page by page, instead of about variant handwritten copies”，即印刷书使各国学者得以逐页讨论同一文本，这是手抄副本无法做到的。B与“literacy rates rose only gradually”矛盾；C与“for decades the new presses were used primarily to reproduce the same books”矛盾；D与“printed books long remained expensive luxuries”矛盾。

passage: Beneath Yellowstone National Park lies one of the largest volcanic systems on Earth, a structure that is neither a cone nor a vent but a vast, roughly circular depression called a caldera, formed when the ground collapsed after a series of enormous eruptions. The most recent of these, about 640,000 years ago, ejected hundreds of cubic kilometers of ash and rock, enough to bury much of the western United States under a layer of volcanic debris. Since then, the system has remained active: magma still rises into a shallow chamber beneath the caldera, heating the park's famous geysers and hot springs, and the ground above the chamber bulges and subsides by centimeters as the magma moves. Monitoring by geologists has detected swarms of small earthquakes and changes in the rate of heat flow, but they stress that such activity is normal for a restless system and that the probability of a major eruption in any given century remains low. The greatest hazard posed by the volcano, they note, is not the eruption itself but its aftermath: a large eruption would blanket the region in ash, disrupting agriculture, transportation, and air quality for years.
question: As used in the passage, the word “caldera” most nearly means
options: a shallow chamber of molten rock beneath the surface
a layer of compacted ash spread over hundreds of kilometers
a circular depression left when the ground collapsed after a huge eruption
a cone-shaped mountain built of alternating lava and ash layers
explanation: 答案C。文中同位语直接给出定义：“a vast, roughly circular depression called a caldera, formed when the ground collapsed after a series of enormous eruptions”，即火山喷发后地面塌陷形成的大型圆形凹陷。B描述的是锥形火山；B是“magma chamber”；C是火山灰层，均不符。

passage: Every autumn, millions of monarch butterflies leave their summer breeding grounds in southern Canada and the northern United States and travel up to four thousand kilometers to a handful of mountain forests in central Mexico. No individual monarch makes the round trip; the butterflies that arrive in Mexico are the great-grandchildren of those that left in spring, and they have never been to the forests before. Scientists have shown that the migrants navigate using a combination of cues: the angle of the sun, adjusted for the time of day by an internal clock in the antennae, and the earth's magnetic field, which provides a backup compass when the sky is overcast. How the genetic program encodes this route is not fully understood, but laboratory studies suggest that the direction of flight is inherited, and that the second and third generations raised in captivity, far from any wild monarch, still attempt to fly in the correct autumn direction when tested. The wintering sites themselves are under threat, as logging thins the fir forests that shelter the dense clusters of resting butterflies and keep them from freezing.
question: The word “they” in the passage refers to
options: the monarch butterflies that arrive in Mexico
the wintering forests in central Mexico
the internal clocks in the antennae
explanation: 答案B。定位句：“the butterflies that arrive in Mexico are the great-grandchildren of those that left in spring, and they have never been to the forests before”，句首主语即“the butterflies that arrive in Mexico”，代词“they”指代这些到达墨西哥的蝴蝶——它们从未到过越冬森林。A、C、D 均非句中主语。

passage: Of the roughly seven thousand languages spoken in the world today, linguists estimate that between a third and a half will fall silent within the next century. The causes are familiar: economic pressure to speak majority languages, urbanization that disperses small communities, and official policies that have historically punished the use of minority tongues in schools. What is lost when a language vanishes is more than a vocabulary: a language encodes a community's accumulated knowledge, its classifications of the natural world, its oral literature, and subtle ways of organizing thought that are not always translatable. Linguists have documented, for example, that some languages encode spatial relations exclusively in terms of absolute directions, forcing speakers to maintain a permanent mental compass, while others preserve taxonomies of local plants and animals that have no equivalent in global scientific nomenclature. Because such knowledge is often held by the oldest speakers, efforts to record endangered languages have become a race against time, with audio archives and dictionaries now being produced in collaboration with communities that are simultaneously working to teach the languages to a new generation.
question: What is the passage mainly about?
options: Most endangered languages are spoken by fewer than one hundred people
Urbanization is the sole cause of language loss worldwide
The loss of languages is erasing irreplaceable knowledge, prompting urgent efforts to document and revive them
Languages that encode spatial directions are impossible to translate into other languages
explanation: 答案C。全段核心是语言消亡的规模（“between a third and a half will fall silent”）、语言承载不可替代的知识（“encodes a community's accumulated knowledge”），以及“efforts to record endangered languages have become a race against time”，C全面概括。A、B过于绝对；D歪曲了“not always translatable”的含义。

passage: The oceans absorb roughly a quarter of the carbon dioxide released into the atmosphere by human activity, a service that slows global warming but exacts a price: as the gas dissolves in seawater, it forms carbonic acid, and the pH of the surface ocean has fallen by about 0.1 units since the industrial revolution—a shift of roughly thirty percent in acidity. The organisms most directly affected are those that build shells and skeletons from calcium carbonate, including corals, mollusks, and many plankton. In more acidic water, carbonate ions become scarcer, and these organisms must expend more energy to build their structures; some species have been shown in laboratory studies to grow thinner shells or to devote less energy to reproduction. The effects are not uniform, however: certain species tolerate the change well, and the ability of populations to adapt over generations remains an open question. Researchers emphasize that the acidification observed so far is small compared with the swings that occurred naturally in the distant past, but the current change is happening far more rapidly, giving ecosystems little time to adjust.
question: According to the passage, how does increased acidity in seawater affect shell-building organisms?
options: It completely dissolves their skeletons within a few months
It makes carbonate ions scarcer, forcing organisms to use more energy to build their structures
It increases the availability of calcium carbonate in the water
It has a uniform effect on all shell-building species
explanation: 答案B。原文写道“In more acidic water, carbonate ions become scarcer, and these organisms must expend more energy to build their structures”。A“completely dissolves... within months”过度且文中未提；C方向相反；D与“The effects are not uniform”直接矛盾。

passage: The great stained-glass windows of the Gothic cathedrals are often admired as triumphs of medieval artistry, but they were also triumphs of engineering.
